opening.headline: Even with input filters and system prompt rules in place, you'll learn how to verify that your defenses are actually working.
body: Just because you add input filters, system prompt rules, and output checks to your service doesn't mean your defenses will work well. The fact that you set it up and the fact that it is actually blocked are two different things. General quality assessments based on questions may not sufficiently address malicious or evasive input.

In this class, we'll look at red teams that intentionally break defenses, what adversarial testing is, how to construct an adversarial evaluation set, and how to use automatic generation and human review together. At the end, the two metrics, attack success rate and normal request rejection rate, are read together, the sample size and adaptive attackers are taken into consideration to determine how trustworthy the numbers are, and the process of adjusting the strength of defense is practiced as an example.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the scope, scenario, and recording method of the red team
The balance between rejection rate and attack success rate can be evaluated.
Can explain the effects of sample size, repeated measurements, and judgment errors on the reliability of evaluation values
Explain the limitations of fixed attack sets and the need for adaptive attacker verification and evaluation for agents.

screens.title: How to know if your defenses are working
screens.lead: Imagine a service that already has defenses in place, and think about how you can check their effectiveness.

paragraphs: Assume that a customer service service has three defenses attached to it. Input filters to filter user input, system prompt rules to limit topic and tone, and output inspection to check responses. It's all written down in the design document and turned on.

But how do we know if this defense actually works? Turning the setting on and actually blocking attack input are two different things. The filter may only catch certain expressions and miss input that has been worded differently, and sentences written with rules may be read differently by the model.

Another difficulty is the input used for evaluation. A typical quality assessment consists of questions that come in on a daily basis. Even if such an evaluation produces good results, malicious or intentionally evasive input may produce different results.
The questions we will answer in this class are: What inputs and what indicators are used to check the effectiveness of defense?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Can we assume that a service that had a high percentage of correct answers in a general evaluation would perform at the same level under adversarial input? Think again at the end of class.

screens.outro: First, let's think about whether we have ever experienced a similar inspection.

screens.title: Think of a similar situation
screens.lead: If you think about the question on your own first and then select it, the instructor will organize it for you. You will not enter or submit an answer. Connect the experience you recall to the concept on the screen later.

items.prompt: Have you ever intentionally tried to break a new feature before releasing it?
items.answer: This includes experiences that intentionally push the system, such as security checks or load tests. The same idea is needed in AI services. Services that have only been confirmed for normal use are likely to have weaknesses revealed by malicious input they encounter for the first time after launch.

items.prompt: Have you ever seen a service go off to a strange topic or easily change the rules?
items.answer: Sometimes the service follows suit when the user asks them to change the subject or ignore previous instructions. Scenes like these that behave differently than the developer intended are what adversarial testing is looking for.

items.prompt: Have you ever been so defensive that you even refused to ask normal questions?
items.answer: If your defense is weak, it's a problem; if it's too strong, it's a problem. When normal questions are rejected, users leave the service or find workarounds. So this lesson covers how to measure both how much an attack is blocked and how much normal requests are blocked.

screens.outro: Now, let’s start by defining what red teaming and adversarial testing are.

screens.title: What are red teams and adversarial testing?
screens.lead: Try alternating between two adversarial queries. Both types, with varying degrees of apparentness, are subject to testing. Only by including both visible and invisible risks will the assessment become closer to reality.

states.label: explicit adversarial query
states.body:
The input contains expressions that violate the policy, or the input is clearly intended to trick the model into saying something dangerous. For example, input that ignores previous instructions and asks you to provide limited information.

These inputs are captured relatively well by filters, so populating the evaluation set with just these types can make the defense appear well-validated. So, it must be included, but it should not be everything. Adversarial testing uses both types of testing to systematically explore how a model reacts to both malicious and inadvertently harmful uses.

The Red Team has a different role from a regular evaluation. Assessments measure whether the system is behaving as intended, while red teams dig into how the system performs under adversarial or unexpected input. As a result, we get a basis for making improvements such as fine-tuning, safety devices, and filters and deciding whether to release it or not.

states.label: Implicit Adversarial Query
states.body:
Input that is seemingly innocuous but touches sensitive topics such as demographics, health, finance, and religion. For example, the question asking whether my religion limits my credit limit may vary. Although there is no policy violation, it is an input that can cause the model to give biased or inappropriate answers.

Because there is no explicit language, keyword-based filters won't catch it. Therefore, both explicit and implicit inputs must be included to broadly identify the actual risk. Additionally, red teams should only perform testing on code and assets that they own or have been explicitly permitted to test.

screens.outro: The above two types are the basic ingredients that make up the evaluation set. Let’s take a closer look at the definition and purpose of a red team.

screens.title: Composition of adversarial evaluation set
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation appears. Check out the elements that a good adversarial evaluation set must have one by one.

data.text: adversarial testing is a systematic way to examine how a model responds to malicious or inadvertently harmful inputs. Red teams complement general evaluations by focusing on abuse cases, failure type, and high-risk interactions. The evaluation set first establishes a foundation based on product policies and failure type. For every prohibited action, there must be a corresponding mitigation mechanism, and the entire set becomes part of the test scope. Subsequently, it includes real-world use cases such as summaries or recommendations, along with rare borderline case. It also encompasses diverse input lengths, vocabularies, and question formats, Vocabulary Diversity, as well as broad topics and identity characteristics, cultural contexts, meaning diversity. Unlike general evaluation sets that reflect real-world distributions, adversarial evaluation sets deliberately include inputs that could cause issues, Out-of-distribution example. The results help identify improvement directions such as fine-tuning, safeguards, and filters, and serve as a basis for launch decisions.

terms.tip: It's a way to systematically learn how a model reacts to malicious or inadvertently harmful input.
This is a breakdown of how services can go wrong. There must be a countermeasure for each prohibited action.
A rare input that lies on the border between normal and transgressive. It can help you determine whether your defenses are too strict or too lax.
The standard is to vary the length, vocabulary, and question formats such as interrogative sentences and direct/indirect requests, and to avoid duplication.
The standard is that each policy covers a wide range of topics, identity characteristics, and cultural rights. Evaluation sets that focus only on specific topics miss weaknesses.
Although it rarely appears in normal input, it is input that can cause problems. The adversarial evaluation set intentionally includes examples like this.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the composition principles, let's look at the flow of actually creating and running an evaluation set.

screens.title: Automatic attack generation and evaluation flow
screens.lead: Take a step-by-step look at the entire process of creating and evaluating an adversarial evaluation set. Select the arrow to go to the next step.

steps.title: 1. Establish a baseline
steps.body: First, we establish a baseline with existing public benchmarks. We check whether the existing evaluation set sufficiently covers the policy scope of our service, and if it is insufficient, we create it ourselves.

steps.title: 2. Create seed data
steps.body: For each category, dozens of pieces of seed data are manually created. Examples written by someone who knows the service's policies and actual usage context determine the quality of subsequent expansions.

steps.title: 3. Expand with synthesis tools
steps.body: Extend Seeds with data synthesis tools. Open source frameworks like Promptfoo help you create adversarial test cases, explore the behavior of your targets, and use the results to improve your system. Automatic creation expands the scope of what humans cannot create individually. However, a human must check the sample to see if the generated cases match the actual policy. In research, there are cases where a language model creates a large number of test inputs and a separate classifier determines whether the target model's response is harmful, thus filling a scale that is difficult for humans to write directly.

steps.title: 4. Annotate the output
steps.body: After creating a model output from the evaluation set input, each output is annotated with the type of failure and type of harm. You need to sort out which policies are broken and how so you can know where to fix them. For example, even for the same injection, the response varies depending on whether it is a departure from the topic or an information leak.

steps.title: 5. Automatic annotation and human verification
steps.body: Annotation is done automatically with a safety classifier, but low-confidence decisions are checked by humans. Automation takes on the role of scale, and humans take on the role of correcting ambiguous judgments. This is because the cost is high if all decisions are made by a human, and if all decisions are made automatically, mistakes made by the classifier will result in the same result.

steps.title: 6. Summarize in a report
steps.body: Results are summarized in reports focusing on safety factors and failure cases. Reports are the basis for determining improvement directions and materials for communicating with stakeholders.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the evaluation flow, let's summarize the safety best practices we put into our service in addition to the evaluation.

ext.title: Perez et al., Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models (2022)
Mazeika et al., HarmBench: A Standardized Evaluation Framework for Automated Red Teaming and Robust Refusal (2024)

screens.title: Safety best practices and results interpretation
screens.lead: The following flashcards illustrate five best practices to complement your defenses. When you select a card, it flips over and you can move to the next card with the right arrow.

cards.back: Let's enter both the representative inputs that the service normally receives and the inputs that we want to intentionally break. Make sure you don't go off topic or be easily fooled by injections that tell you to ignore previous instructions. Doing it before launch is key. This is because if weaknesses are revealed after the number of people using the service increases, damage has already occurred.

If possible, have a human review the output before actually writing it. This is especially important in high-risk areas and code generation. It is important that reviewers are aware of the limitations of the system and have easy access to the original. Any service that summarizes notes should allow you to view the original notes right away. If you only ask for review without providing a basis for confirmation, people will end up believing the model's answer.

Limiting the length a user can input reduces the risk of injection, and limiting output tokens reduces the potential for misuse. It is safer to use verified options instead of free input, or to select and return answers from verified data rather than creating new ones. For example, instead of creating an answer to a customer's question, you can link to an existing guidance document that best matches the question.

It allows you to track user-specific activity, helping you respond quickly when misuse occurs. It is used to identify which users are repeatedly causing problems and take action. Without the ability to identify users, it is easy for one person's misuse to lead to restrictions on the entire service.

Evaluation results are organized into safety factors, failure cases, and mitigation measures. It is data for communication not only with the development team but also with stakeholders, and serves as a standard for comparison during the next evaluation. By writing down specific failures, you can quickly recognize when the same problem occurs again.

screens.outro: Now, let's use examples to practice reading two key indicators.

screens.title: Commentary: Read Rejection Rate and Attack Success Rate
screens.lead: Move the slider to change the strength of your defense. The instructor explains how the two indicators vary depending on intensity. The numbers on the screen are assumptions for illustrative purposes only. The last two points consider how trustworthy the numbers can be.

stops.body: Assumed figures: 40% attack success rate, 1% normal request rejection rate. The attack success rate is the percentage of adversarial inputs in which the model responded by violating the policy, and the normal request rejection rate is the percentage of legitimate questions that were incorrectly blocked. This setup is smooth for the user, but four out of ten attack inputs pass through. You should not assume that something is safe just because normal requests are rarely blocked.

Assumed figures: 12% attack success rate, 4% normal request rejection rate. Most known patterns are blocked and some legitimate requests are alerted. Both indicators are at a medium level, so they are often used as a starting point. From here, adjust up or down depending on which metrics are more important to you.

Assumed figures: 3% attack success rate, 18% normal request rejection rate. The attack is almost always blocked, but almost one in five normal questions is incorrectly rejected. User inconvenience is great and service value is reduced. If you look at the attack success rate numbers alone, it looks like a successful setup, which is why you need to look at the rejection rate as well. The fact that one number has improved does not mean that the entire service has improved.

Increasing the defense strength lowers the attack success rate, but increases the normal request rejection rate. In high-risk tasks, you can focus on lowering the attack success rate, and in general counseling, you can focus on lowering the rejection rate. You need to look at both indicators at once; if you only look at one, you miss out on over- or under-defense. The numbers in the table are only illustrative assumptions; actual values ​​should be measured directly with your own evaluation set. If the composition of the evaluation set is different, even for the same defense, the numbers will be different.

If the evaluation set is small, the numbers fluctuate significantly. Assuming, in an evaluation set with only 50 adversarial inputs, 2 successful attacks are 4%, and 3 successful attacks are 6%. Since the two numbers are separated by one case, this difference cannot be read as evidence that defense has worsened or improved. Since the model's answer may vary even with the same input, the same evaluation is repeated several times and the average and variation range (confidence interval) are viewed together. As the sample size increases, the amount of variation decreases. Also, since the automatic classifier or LLM screening that determines success or failure may be wrong, some samples are re-checked by humans to determine the extent of the judgment error. Only through this process can you determine whether the difference between the two indicators is real or coincidental.

If the attack you're evaluating is fixed, it's easy for the defense to adjust to that set and make the numbers look good. One study tested twelve defenses as an adaptive attack that changes and optimizes the attack according to the design of the defense. Most defenses were breached with success rates exceeding 90%, many of which were defenses that originally reported success rates close to 0% in their fixed attack set. So, the low attack success rate is read together with the value obtained from which attack set, and after changing the defense, a new attack is created and verified again. The same evaluation set is used to compare before and after, and adaptive revalidation is a separate check.

screens.outro: Now that you know how to read the indicators, let's take a step-by-step look at making decisions to adjust your defense based on the results of your evaluation.

ext.title: Nasr et al., The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections (2025)
Mazeika et al., HarmBench: A Standardized Evaluation Framework for Automated Red Teaming and Robust Refusal (2024)

screens.title: Commentary: Judgment to adjust defense based on evaluation results
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process by which the team adjusts its defense after receiving the evaluation results. Follow the order of judgment by going through the steps with the arrows.

steps.title: check the situation
steps.body: As a result of the evaluation, some of the injection inputs passed and some of the normal questions were also rejected. Since you have two problems at the same time, you need to decide which one to fix first.

steps.title: Step 1. Break it down by failure type
steps.body: Divide the attacks that passed and the normal requests that were rejected by failure type to see where they were breached and what rules blocked the normal requests. If you only look at the overall numbers, you won't be able to tell the cause. Even for the same injection, it is necessary to distinguish by layer whether the input check was missed or the system prompt rule was weak.

steps.title: Step 2. Strengthen input checking and reflect it in thresholds
steps.body: Enhances input validation to match the type of attack passed. At the same time, incorrectly rejected normal question cases are collected and reflected in the threshold adjustment. The reason for combining strengthening and mitigation is to improve both indicators. This is because if only one side is tightened, other indicators will worsen.

steps.title: Step 3. Run the same evaluation set again
steps.body: After adjustment, run the same evaluation set again and compare the changes in attack success rate and normal request rejection rate. If you change the evaluation set, you cannot tell whether the change is a result of an adjustment or a difference in the evaluation set. Maintaining comparable conditions is fundamental to evaluation. Additionally, recording the model and configuration versions before and after adjustments can help you track which changes have had an effect.

steps.title: Step 4. Make sure your measurements are reliable
steps.body: Rather than immediately jumping to conclusions that the numbers have changed, check to see if your sample size is large enough. If the evaluation set is small, the ratio may vary significantly by just one or two cases. The same evaluation is repeated to see the range of variation, and errors in the automatic classifier that determines success are also assessed by human checking some samples. If the change is within the fluctuation range, it cannot be assumed that it is an effect of adjustment.

steps.title: Step 5. Verify again with adaptive attacks
steps.body: Improvements in a fixed evaluation set do not rule out the possibility that the defense has been tailored to that set. Just as an attacker who knows the design of a defense changes the attack, he creates new variants and revalidates them. At this time, if an unblocked type is found, it is added to the evaluation set and used for the next comparison.

steps.title: Step 6. If you are an agent, look at the success rate of your work.
steps.body: For an agent using a tool, it is more important than whether the text was rejected, rather than whether the user performed the task assigned to him/her even if an attack occurred. So, we look at the task success rate when there is no attack, the task success rate when there is an attack, and the attack success rate together. This is the agent version of the normal request rejection rate. As an open evaluation environment, AgentDojo measures both task success and attack success using 97 realistic tasks such as email management, e-banking, and travel booking, and 629 security test cases. InjecAgent evaluates indirect injection of tooled agents in 1,054 test cases. There are also evaluations that measure excessive rejection separately. XSTest consists of 250 safe questions to avoid and 200 risky questions to prepare for, catching the tendency to overly reject safe questions.

steps.title: Step 7. record and update
steps.body: The results are recorded in a report, and the evaluation set is updated whenever the product changes. Because with new features and new policies come new failure types. If you keep using the evaluation set you created once, you will miss out on new risks. The evaluation set itself is also subject to inspection.

screens.outro: Finally, we organize the entire class. Remember, the evaluation doesn't end once; it continues to be updated along with the product.

Zhan et al., InjecAgent: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated Large Language Model Agents (2024)
Röttger et al., XSTest: A Test Suite for Identifying Exaggerated Safety Behaviours in Large Language Models (2023)
Nasr et al., The Attacker Moves Second (2025)

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: The defense verification flow is connected and organized into one.

paragraphs: To know if your defenses are working, you have to try to break them on purpose. Red teams use adversarial input to identify abuse cases and high-risk interactions that regular quality assessments miss, and they complement assessments rather than replace them. A mature evaluation system uses the two together.

The adversarial evaluation set is designed to have diversity in product policies and failure types, use cases and boundary cases, and vocabulary and semantics. This includes explicit queries as well as seemingly harmless implicit queries. Automated generation broadens scope and human review corrects uncertain judgments. All these results are reported and compared to the next evaluation.

The attack success rate and normal request rejection rate must be viewed together. If we only look at one side, we miss excessive or under-defense. The answer to the first question, whether good general evaluation results are safe from adversarial input, is no. Defenses must be checked directly against adversarial input. This judgment habit is the core of this class.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Think about what type of input you want to break first in your service, and whether that type is explicit or implicit. Consider also whether there is now a way to check whether that input actually breaches the defense.

glossary.def: This is an activity that attempts to break a system from the perspective of an actual attacker and finds vulnerabilities. Supplements general assessment.
A collection of inputs for testing that may lead to policy violations or malfunctions.
This is the percentage of adversarial inputs that broke through defenses and the model responded by violating policy.
What percentage of legitimate questions are incorrectly rejected?
It stands for human in the loop, and is a method in which a person reviews the output before actually writing it.
This is an attack that optimizes by knowing the design of the defense and changing the attack accordingly. It is used to re-verify low success rates from a fixed attack set.

misconceptions.myth: It has passed the general evaluation, so it is safe.
misconceptions.fact: The general evaluation is centered around questions, so it may not be able to sufficiently address malicious or circumstantial input. Adversarial evaluation complements this.

misconceptions.myth: If you collect only highly toxic sentences, it becomes an evaluation set.
misconceptions.fact: The filter catches explicit expressions well. It should also include implicit input that is seemingly innocuous but touches on sensitive topics.

misconceptions.myth: Increasing the rejection rate makes it safer.
misconceptions.fact: If normal requests are blocked, user inconvenience increases. A balance must be determined by looking at the attack success rate and the normal request rejection rate together.

misconceptions.myth: The attack success rate has dropped to 3%, so the defense has been fully verified.
misconceptions.fact: If the evaluation set is small, the numbers may fluctuate by one or two cases, and the defense may be tailored to a fixed set of attacks. Sample size, replication, judgment errors, and re-validation results with adaptive attacks should also be read together.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Red Teams are adversarial checks that supplement regular assessments.
The adversarial evaluation set is designed based on policy scope and diversity.
Automatic generation and human review are combined, and the results are left in a report.
Defense strength is determined by balancing attack success rate and normal request rejection rate, but taking into account sample size and judgment errors.
The results from the fixed attack set are re-verified using adaptive attacks, and the agent also measures the task success rate.
